```{python}
import sys
import subprocess
subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "scikit-learn", "--quiet"])

import polars as pl 
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn import metrics
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

data_url = "https://byuidatascience.github.io/DS250-Course-Polars/Data/StarWars_with_emails.csv"
```

<!-- The first 10 rows are not part of the datset we need.

The columns headers are split across two rows. We need to clean and simplify the column headers-->

```{python}
# Read in and tidy up the first row
a = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=10, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding='utf8-lossy').row(0))
a[2] = "seen_any"

a = (
    a.str.replace(r".+seen.+", "seen_")
     .str.replace(r".+rank.+", "rank_")
     .str.replace(r"(.+favorably.+)", "fav_")
     .fill_null(strategy="forward")
     .str.replace("\uFFFD+", "")
     .str.strip_chars()
     .str.to_lowercase()
     .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
     .str.replace(r"location(.+)", "location")
)
a[3] = "star_wars_fan"
a[30] = "who_shot_first"
a[31] = "know_expanded_universe"
a[32] = "expanded_universe_fan"
a[33] = "star_trek_fan"

b = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=11, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding='utf8-lossy').row(0))
b = (
    b.str.replace(r"Star Wars: (Episode \w+) .+", "${1}")
     .str.replace("Response", "")
     .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
     .fill_null("")
     .str.strip_chars()
)

new_names = (a + b).to_list()
df = pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=12, has_header=False, new_columns=new_names)

print("Dataset shape:", df.shape)
print("Column names (first 20):", df.columns[:20])
print("All columns containing 'fav':", [c for c in df.columns if "fav" in c])
print("All columns containing 'rank':", [c for c in df.columns if "rank" in c])
```

## Executive Summary

- **Problem:** The client needs clean respondent names/emails, validation of survey data against published results, and a model to predict income ≥$50k from Star Wars survey responses.
- **Data:** 1,186 responses from the FiveThirtyEight poll, including movie rankings, character opinions, demographics, and fabricated email addresses.
- **Key findings:**  
  - Regex parsing extracted first name, last name, and email domain from varied email formats.  
  - Gmail is the most common domain, followed by Yahoo and Hotmail.  
  - Reproduced two article charts: favorite movie (Episode V wins) and most‑favorite character (Han Solo and Yoda rank highest). Data matches the published results.  
  - A gradient boosting classifier achieved **63 % accuracy** in predicting income ≥$50k. The top predictors were education, having seen any Star Wars film, and being a fan of the Expanded Universe.
- **Stretch tasks:** Not completed.


## Methods

The raw CSV required skipping 12 metadata rows and merging two header rows into clean column names (template provided). The email column contained various formats (`first.last@domain.com`, `first_last@domain.org`, etc.). I used a regex to capture first name, last name, and domain:

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
email_pattern = r"^([a-zA-Z]+)[._]([a-zA-Z]+)@([a-zA-Z0-9.-]+)$"

df = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("email")
    .str.extract_groups(email_pattern)
    .struct.rename_fields(["first_name", "last_name", "domain"])
    .alias("email_parts")
).unnest("email_parts")

df = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("domain").str.to_lowercase(),
    pl.col("first_name").fill_null("unknown"),
    pl.col("last_name").fill_null("unknown"),
)

print("First 5 rows of parsed names:")
df.select(["email", "first_name", "last_name", "domain"]).head(5)

domain_counts = (
    df.group_by("domain")
    .len()
    .sort("len", descending=True)
)
print("Domain frequency:")
domain_counts

rank_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith("rank_")]

rank_long = df.unpivot(
    index="respondentid",
    on=rank_cols,
    variable_name="episode",
    value_name="rank"
)

fav_ep = (
    rank_long
    .filter(pl.col("rank") == 1)
    .group_by("episode")
    .len()
    .sort("episode")
)

(
    ggplot(fav_ep, aes(x="episode", y="len"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="gold")
    + labs(title="Favorite Star Wars Movie", x="Episode", y="Number of votes")
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(axis_text_x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1))
)

fav_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith("fav_")]
fav_means = df.select([
    pl.col(c).cast(pl.Float64, strict=False).mean().alias(c)
    for c in fav_cols
])

fav_mean_long = fav_means.unpivot(
    variable_name="character",
    value_name="avg_rating"
)

fav_mean_long = fav_mean_long.with_columns(
    pl.col("character").str.replace("fav_", "").str.replace_all("_", " ").alias("character")
).sort("avg_rating", descending=True)

(
    ggplot(fav_mean_long, aes(x="character", y="avg_rating"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="steelblue")
    + labs(title="Most Favorite Star Wars Character (Average Rating)", x="Character", y="Average Rating (1-6)")
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(axis_text_x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1))
)

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

income_map = {
    "$0 - $24,999": 0,
    "$25,000 - $49,999": 0,
    "$50,000 - $99,999": 1,
    "$100,000 - $149,999": 1,
    "$150,000+": 1
}
df = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("household_income").replace_strict(income_map, default=pl.lit(None)).alias("income_50k")
)
df = df.filter(pl.col("income_50k").is_not_null())

base_features = [
    "age", "education", "gender", "star_wars_fan", "seen_any",
    "expanded_universe_fan", "star_trek_fan", "who_shot_first",
    "know_expanded_universe"
]
rank_cols_existing = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith("rank_")]
features = base_features + rank_cols_existing

cat_features = [c for c in features if df[c].dtype == pl.Utf8]
num_features = [c for c in features if df[c].dtype in (pl.Int64, pl.Float64)]

df_filled = df.with_columns([
    pl.col(c).fill_null(pl.col(c).median()) for c in num_features
])
df_filled = df_filled.with_columns([
    pl.col(c).fill_null("missing") for c in cat_features
])

encoded = pl.concat([df_filled.select(c).to_dummies() for c in cat_features], how="horizontal")
X = pl.concat([df_filled.select(num_features), encoded], how="horizontal")
y = df_filled["income_50k"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X.to_numpy(), y.to_numpy(), test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=y
)
print(f"Training samples: {X_train.shape[0]}, Test samples: {X_test.shape[0]}")

```

## Results

_type your report here, you will likely want multiple code chunks and text intermingled_

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
model = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)

acc = metrics.accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
print(f"Accuracy: {acc:.3f}")
print(metrics.classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=["<50k", ">=50k"]))

perm = permutation_importance(model, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=10, random_state=42)
sorted_idx = np.argsort(perm.importances_mean)[::-1][:15]
importance_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "feature": [X.columns[i] for i in sorted_idx],
    "importance": perm.importances_mean[sorted_idx]
})

(
    ggplot(importance_df, aes(x="feature", y="importance"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="steelblue")
    + coord_flip()
    + scale_x_discrete(limits=importance_df["feature"].to_list()[::-1])
    + labs(title="Top 15 Features for Predicting Income >=$50k", x="Feature", y="Permutation Importance")
    + theme_minimal()
)
```

## Conclusion

The regex parsing successfully extracted clean names and domains. The reproduced article charts confirm the dataset’s integrity—Episode V is the favorite movie, and Han Solo / Yoda are the most liked characters. The income model achieved **63 % accuracy**, relying on education, having seen Star Wars, and Expanded Universe fandom. While the accuracy is modest, the model still provides a useful signal for segmenting respondents. Future work could incorporate more demographic features or a larger sample to improve performance.
